neighbours.label: The connective that justifies a piece of advice ('just in case', 'you never know', 'in case of', 'because'), vs the same words in narration or legal/descriptive use
fire: Pack a spare charger, you never know when the battery will die.
Write down the address on paper just in case your phone breaks.
Keep a fire extinguisher in the kitchen in case of a grease fire.
Always carry some water on the trail, you never know how long it will take.
Lock your bike even for a minute, because thieves move fast.
Take a sweater along just in case the evening gets cold.
Leave early for the airport in case of heavy traffic.
Back up your photos tonight, you never know what might happen.
quiet: The lawyer said that in this case the contract was void.
My grandfather never knew his own father.
The extinguisher in the kitchen was red and quite heavy.
In that case, the judge decided to postpone the hearing.
The bike was stolen on Tuesday outside the library.
She wore a sweater to the concert last night.
The airport was busy on the morning we left.
He looked at his old photos and smiled.

predictions: Advice followed by a precautionary or reason clause 0.5-1.3; 'case', 'know', 'because' in narration under 0.15.
notes: Card: ' know' in 'you never know', ' case' in 'just in case', ' because' after a warning. Probe: 'you never know when you might need it' 1.280, 'just in case it rains' 0.723, 'to pay the parking fee' 0.657, 'in case of overheating' 0.532, 'just to be safe' 0.532, 'because it is raining' 0.466; 'In this case the court' 0.004, floor 0.008.
